title: The verse you keep
hookLine: choose one verse from the juz' to carry for good

lines: A NOTE FOLDED IN A WALLET.
ONE VERSE TO TAKE WITH YOU.
cards: Some people keep a note folded in a wallet for years: a line from a letter, a thing a teacher once said. The paper goes soft at the creases. They don't read it every day.

They just know it's there, and on the worst days they take it out. One night, Abu Dharr reports, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stood in prayer and recited a single verse, over and over, until dawn. One verse, a whole night.
You've now read thirty-seven surahs, and tomorrow this camp closes. Before it does, one thing to take with you: not the whole juz', but one verse from it, kept like that folded note.

teach.b: An early report says the companions would take ten verses at a time and not move on until they knew them and had lived them.
A kept verse works the same way: not a quotation to admire, but a line that does a job in your life. Here are three from the part you've read.
From Ash-Sharh, Surah ninety-four, in Pickthall: But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease. Two things.
The word is with, ma'a, not after, and some readers take that to mean the ease is already inside the hard thing, not only waiting beyond it. And the line is said twice.

Commentators noticed that hardship has the definite article, the hardship, while ease does not, so they read it as one hardship and two eases. A report from Ibn Abbas puts it: one hardship will not overcome two eases.
From Ad-Duha, Surah ninety-three, words to the Prophet, tradition says, in a dry season when revelation had paused: your Lord has not forsaken you, nor does He hate you.
And from Az-Zalzalah, Surah ninety-nine: And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then. Nothing is too small to count. One for the hard day, one for the lonely day, one for the ordinary day.
But the verse you keep doesn't have to be any of these. It might be the whisperer that withdraws, or sleep as a sign. The only test is whether you'll take it out when you need it.

how: Favorite verses are kept close: written in calligraphy on walls, memorized to recite in hard moments, or repeated in night prayer; some people return to one verse again and again, as the Prophet is reported to have done.

o: after: ease comes once hardship ends

games.q: the kept verses — tap the pairs.
p: your Lord has not forsaken you

s: Surah 94 says ease comes after hardship
it says with: ma'a. some read the ease as already inside the hard thing.
the Prophet once repeated a single verse through a whole night
commentators read 94:5–6 as two eases for one hardship
hardship is definite, ease is not; a report from Ibn Abbas says so.

games.q: a hard season comes. which verse from the juz' says the ease is already inside it?
games.why: 94:5–6: with hardship, ease, said twice. ma'a means with, not after.

practice: Let the verses of these weeks pass through your mind like cards being shuffled, and wait, not for the most impressive one, but for the one that pulls at you, that seems to know something about your life right now.
When it comes, say it silently on the in-breath and let it settle on the out-breath. If you like, imagine folding it small and putting it somewhere safe inside you.

wordCard.voice: Ma'a, with: the word in Ash-Sharh that says ease comes with hardship, not only after it.

orig.note: Arabic: truly, with hardship is ease (94:5–6).

carryVoice: Your line: one verse, kept. Folded small, it goes wherever you go. Day two hundred thirty, done.
